Getting started with poolinfo

Source: vignettes/poolinfo.Rmd
poolinfo.Rmd

In a multisite trial each site gives an estimate of the intervention’s effect, with a standard error. A hierarchical model shrinks each estimate toward the overall mean, a noisy site’s estimate more than a precise one’s. poolinfo summarizes this shrinkage across all the sites of a trial. The summaries are worth a look before you rank the sites, report their effects or study how the effect varies among them, because they say how much of each site’s own estimate survives in the model’s results, and they bear on which estimator suits such a goal (Lee 2026). In this vignette we analyze one outcome of a real trial, from the site estimates to the report.

library(poolinfo)

The data

The Online Credit Recovery Study randomized students who had failed Algebra 1 or English 9 in their first year of high school to one of two summer courses at their school, an online course or the school’s usual teacher-directed course (Rickles et al. 2024). The data set ocrs has one row for each of the 32 school-by-subject sites in which students were assigned to both courses.

head(ocrs[, c("site", "subject", "n", "estimate", "se")])
#>   site   subject  n    estimate         se
#> 1  S01 Algebra 1 57  0.20526372 0.13001694
#> 2  S02 Algebra 1 47 -0.27638587 0.10163046
#> 3  S03 Algebra 1 58  0.03845466 0.09179922
#> 4  S04 Algebra 1 39 -0.12344656 0.16209038
#> 5  S05 Algebra 1 41 -0.01560407 0.15503087
#> 6  S06 Algebra 1 38  0.06041924 0.17049175

Each estimate is the effect of assignment to the online course on passing the course, as a difference in proportions, and se is its standard error. A negative estimate means that, in that site, a smaller proportion of the students assigned to the online course passed. Within a site, the estimate comes from a regression of passing on the assignment indicator and the randomization blocks, so it weights the blocks differently from a comparison of all the site’s students. ?ocrs gives the details, and vignette("multisite-trial") compares this contrast with other first-stage analyses.

Fitting the posterior

reliability_posterior() takes the estimates and their standard errors. We also record the scale of the effects and the estimand at each site, which the printed output and the report sentences repeat.

fit <- reliability_posterior(
  estimate, se = se, site = site, data = ocrs,
  scale_label = "risk difference",
  target_label = "the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course passing"
)
fit
#> Reliability profile of 32 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(mean, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the mean and on sigma_tau
#> Scale of the effects: risk difference
#> Site estimates: the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course
#>                 passing
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                              mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I          0.671    0.497    0.812
#>   mean reliability           0.663    0.498    0.801
#>   dispersion H               0.0253   0.0185   0.0289
#>   concentration count J_eff  31.2     30.3     31.7     of 32
#>   logit variance V           0.237    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                  0.188    0.127    0.266
#>   effect mean                -0.130   -0.211   -0.0498
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                0.973
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)        0.691

We use flat priors on the mean and on the between-site standard deviation στ\sigma_\tau, as Lee (2026) does, and the posterior comes from numerical integration over στ\sigma_\tau in a fraction of a second. See vignette("posterior-summaries") for other priors and how much they matter. The last two lines of the header state an assumption and a definition. The model treats the standard errors as exact, although they are estimates too, so the posterior intervals leave out the uncertainty in the standard errors themselves, and a different first-stage analysis of the same trial could give different diagnostics. And each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size, so a site of 24 students weighs as much as one of 104.

Site reliabilities

Write τ̂j\hat\tau_j for site jj’s estimate and vjv_j for its sampling variance, the squared standard error. Given στ\sigma_\tau and the mean μ\mu of the effects, the posterior mean of site jj’s effect is

Sjτ̂j+(1−Sj)μ,Sj=στ2στ2+vj. S_j \hat\tau_j + (1 - S_j)\mu, \qquad S_j = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j}.

SjS_j is the weight that the normal model puts on the site’s own estimate, and it is also the reliability of the site’s estimate, the proportion of the estimate’s variance that comes from the true effects. We call the reliabilities S1,…,SJS_1, \dots, S_J together the trial’s reliability profile. Lee (2026) writes σ2\sigma^2 and τ\tau for what this package calls στ2\sigma_\tau^2 and μ\mu.

The informativeness

The first summary of the profile is the informativeness,

I=στ2στ2+GM(v), I = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + \mathrm{GM}(v)},

the reliability of a site whose sampling variance is the geometric mean GM(v)\mathrm{GM}(v) of the vjv_j. It is also the mean of the reliabilities on the logit scale (Lee 2026), and Lee et al. (2025) use it to organize comparisons of prior models and posterior summaries for site effects.

For course passing, the posterior mean of II is 0.67, with a 95% posterior interval from 0.50 to 0.81. The geometric mean of the 32 standard errors is 0.128, and the posterior mean of στ\sigma_\tau is 0.19, so στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is about 2.2 times GM(v)\mathrm{GM}(v). A site with the geometric-mean standard error keeps about 67% of its own estimate, which means that the model moves its posterior mean about 33% of the way toward the mean effect. The posterior probability that II exceeds 1/2 is 0.97. At I=1/2I = 1/2, στ2\sigma_\tau^2 equals GM(v)\mathrm{GM}(v) and a site with the geometric-mean standard error is pulled halfway.

Meta-analysts will recognize the form of the I2I^2 statistic (Higgins and Thompson 2002), which puts the “typical” sampling variance where II puts the geometric mean. For these estimates, metafor’s REML fit gives an I2I^2 of 69%, and its estimate of στ\sigma_\tau, 0.179, is a little below the posterior mean.

How unequal the reliabilities are

The other three summaries describe how the reliabilities differ from site to site, and all three depend on the logit variance VV, the variance of the logits of the reliabilities (with divisor JJ). Because logitSj=log⁡στ2−log⁡vj\mathrm{logit}\, S_j = \log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j, VV is also the variance of log⁡vj\log v_j, so the standard errors fix it. Here V=0.24V = 0.24, so the standard errors are typically within a factor of 1.28 of their geometric mean, although they range from 0.077 to 0.218.

The mean reliability S‾\bar S is the ordinary average of the SjS_j. With στ\sigma_\tau and μ\mu known, the average posterior variance of the site effects is στ2(1−S‾)\sigma_\tau^2(1 - \bar S). In a trial whose sites all had the geometric-mean standard error, every SjS_j would equal II, so S‾>I\bar S > I exactly when the site effects are estimated more precisely, on average, than in that trial of equal precision. For passing, S‾\bar S is 0.66, a little below II.

The dispersion HH measures how far the reliabilities are from one another. Treat each SjS_j as the success probability of a Bernoulli distribution, a device for measuring how far apart reliabilities are rather than a model for the data. Among constant values pp, the average Kullback-Leibler divergence J−1∑jKL{Ber(p)∥Ber(Sj)}J^{-1}\sum_j \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\} is smallest at p=Ip = I, and HH is that smallest value. It is 0 only when all the reliabilities are equal. When they are close to one another, the leading terms in VV are

H≈12I(1−I)V,S‾−I≈12I(1−I)(1−2I)V. H \approx \tfrac12 I(1 - I)V, \qquad \bar S - I \approx \tfrac12 I(1 - I)(1 - 2I)V.

The mean reliability is therefore usually below II when I>1/2I > 1/2 and above it when I<1/2I < 1/2, but a skewed profile, or a value of II near 1/2, can reverse the sign. vignette("reliability-profiles") shows when. For passing, the leading term of HH at the posterior mean of II is 0.026, close to HH’s posterior mean of 0.025.

The concentration count

Jeff=(∑jSj)2∑jSj2 J_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_j S_j)^2}{\sum_j S_j^2}

describes how the total reliability ∑jSj\sum_j S_j is shared among the sites. It equals JJ when every site has the same reliability, whatever that reliability is, and it approaches 1 as one site comes to carry nearly all of it. Its formula is Kish’s, with the reliabilities as weights, but it is not a sample size. It measures only how evenly the total is shared, so sites that all have a reliability of 0.1 give JJ, and so do sites that all have 0.9. For passing it is 31.2 of 32, so the total is shared almost evenly.

The posterior in more detail

summary() adds the posterior standard deviations and medians, the posterior of στ\sigma_\tau and of the mean, and each diagnostic’s value at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2.

summary(fit)
#> Reliability profile of 32 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(mean, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the mean and on sigma_tau
#> Scale of the effects: risk difference
#> Site estimates: the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course
#>                 passing
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#> Diagnostics
#>                              mean      sd        2.5%      50%       97.5%
#>   informativeness I          0.671     0.081     0.497     0.677     0.812
#>   mean reliability           0.663     0.078     0.498     0.668     0.801
#>   harmonic centroid          0.644     0.084     0.467     0.650     0.793
#>   dispersion H               0.0253    0.0029    0.0185    0.0258    0.0289
#>   concentration count J_eff  31.2      0.4       30.3      31.2      31.7
#>   logit variance V           0.237     (fixed by the standard errors)
#> 
#> Between-site SD and mean
#>                              mean      sd        2.5%      50%       97.5%
#>   sigma_tau                  0.188     0.0354    0.127     0.185     0.266
#>   sigma_tau^2                0.0365    0.0141    0.0162    0.0342    0.0706
#>   effect mean                -0.130    0.0409    -0.211    -0.131    -0.0498
#> 
#> Pr(I > 0.5) = 0.973
#> 
#> Posterior means and values at the posterior mean of sigma_tau^2
#>                                      posterior at E(sigma_tau^2)
#>   informativeness I                  0.671     0.691
#>   mean reliability                   0.663     0.682
#>   dispersion H                       0.0253    0.0253
#>   concentration count J_eff          31.2      31.3
#> 
#> H is largest, at 0.0289, where sigma_tau = 0.130 (I = 0.509).
#> At that sigma_tau the mean reliability equals I.
#> Integration over sigma_tau: a rule of 800 nodes.
#> All numerical checks are within their limits.

The first block also gives the harmonic centroid, the harmonic mean of the SjS_j, which equals στ2/(στ2+v‾)\sigma_\tau^2/(\sigma_\tau^2 + \bar v) with v‾\bar v the arithmetic mean of the vjv_j, so it is never above II or S‾\bar S. To use the numbers in your own code, profile_summary() returns them as a data frame, one row per quantity.

print(profile_summary(fit), digits = 3)
#>      quantity    mean      sd   lower   upper
#> 1           I  0.6709 0.08079  0.4974  0.8122
#> 2        mean  0.6635 0.07775  0.4980  0.8013
#> 3    harmonic  0.6445 0.08362  0.4672  0.7930
#> 4           H  0.0253 0.00286  0.0185  0.0289
#> 5       J_eff 31.1704 0.35109 30.3456 31.7004
#> 6           V  0.2369 0.00000  0.2369  0.2369
#> 7   sigma_tau  0.1879 0.03538  0.1272  0.2658
#> 8  sigma_tau2  0.0365 0.01411  0.0162  0.0706
#> 9 effect_mean -0.1305 0.04089 -0.2111 -0.0498

The mean effect has posterior mean -13.0 percentage points, with a 95% posterior interval from -21.1 to -5.0. It is the mean of the distribution of site effects, a mean over sites rather than students, so it is not the effect for the average student. Because its interval lies below 0, we conclude that assignment to the online course lowered passing in the average site.

In the last block we compare each posterior mean with the diagnostic’s value at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2, the number that a plug-in of that estimate would report. II and every SjS_j are concave functions of στ2\sigma_\tau^2, so II and S‾\bar S at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 are never below their posterior means (Lee 2026, Proposition 3). Here II is 0.691 against 0.671. HH and JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} have no such order. A plug-in of another estimate of στ\sigma_\tau can fall on either side of the posterior mean: at metafor’s REML estimate, II is 0.663.

Plots

plot() shows four panels: the estimates beside the posterior means of the site effects, the sorted reliabilities, the posterior density of II, and the analysis’s position in the plane of II and VV. We multiply the effects by 100 to show them in percentage points.

plot(fit, scale = 100)

In panel (a) we see the posterior means pulled toward the mean effect, most visibly for the sites with wide intervals. Panel (b) shows the reliability profile, from 0.42 to 0.84. In panel (d) the point lies right of 1/2, where the leading term of S‾−I\bar S - I is negative, and between the contours at 0.02 and 0.03 of HH’s leading term. The plot is a patchwork of ggplot objects. To change one panel, call its own function (plot_pooling(), plot_profile(), plot_functionals() or plot_plane()), which returns a ggplot object with a fuller caption.

The sites

site_table() gives the numbers behind panels (a) and (b), one row per site. We show the three sites with the largest standard errors and the three with the smallest, in percentage points:

sites <- site_table(fit)
sites <- sites[order(sites$se, decreasing = TRUE),
               c("site", "estimate", "se", "reliability", "effect")]
shown <- rbind(head(sites, 3), tail(sites, 3))
points <- c("estimate", "se", "effect")
shown[points] <- round(100 * shown[points], 1)
shown$reliability <- round(shown$reliability, 2)
shown
#>    site estimate   se reliability effect
#> 24  S24    -41.0 21.8        0.42  -24.8
#> 14  S14    -22.2 20.1        0.46  -17.3
#> 18  S18    -23.1 18.8        0.49  -18.0
#> 22  S22    -33.1  9.3        0.79  -28.9
#> 3   S03      3.8  9.2        0.80    0.4
#> 19  S19    -45.3  7.7        0.84  -40.3

Each posterior mean moves toward the mean effect by about 1−Sj1 - S_j of the distance between the site’s estimate and the mean. A noisy site moves a larger part of the way, but it moves far only if its estimate is far from the mean. Site S24, with the largest standard error, moves 58% of the way, from -41.0 to -24.8 points. Site S14 is nearly as noisy and moves 54% of the way, yet its estimate is close to the mean, so its posterior mean changes by only 4.9 points.

Your own data

The same call works for any estimates with standard errors. You can give

  • plain vectors, reliability_posterior(y, se = s), or sampling variances with se2, such as the vi column that metafor::escalc() computes;
  • a random-effects fit of metafor, reliability_posterior(rma_fit), whose moderators become the mean model; reliability_profile(rma_fit) gives the profile at its REML estimate, and vignette("meta-analysis") works through an example;
  • site covariates for the mean, mean_model = ~ x, so that each site is shrunk toward its predicted value;
  • posterior draws of στ\sigma_\tau from other software, to reliability_draws(), which also reads a brms fit of the form y | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | site) directly.

The model treats the sites as independent. In this trial 8 schools have a site in each subject, and some students appear in both. We check how much that matters in vignette("multisite-trial").

The model also gives every site the same mean and variance of the effects, whatever its precision. When the smaller sites tend to have larger effects, say, that common mean and variance can be inadequate (Lee 2026, sec. 9). A plot of the estimates against their standard errors is a first check, although both are noisy:

ggplot2::ggplot(ocrs, ggplot2::aes(x = se, y = estimate)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Standard error", y = "Site estimate") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

In this trial the estimates show no trend with their standard errors (a correlation of -0.06). A trend would call for a covariate in the mean model that carries it, or for a model in which the variance of the effects depends on precision, which poolinfo does not fit.

Reporting

Lee (2026) recommends that a report

  1. state the estimand at each site, its scale, the estimator and the standard errors;
  2. give II and S‾\bar S together, with HH or VV;
  3. add JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} when the concentration of the reliability matters.

report_text() writes the numbers as sentences, with the labels and the conditioning on the standard errors. A report still needs to define the four quantities and cite the paper.

writeLines(strwrap(report_text(fit, outcome = "course passing")))
#> The effects are on the risk difference scale.
#> The estimand at each site is the block-adjusted intention-to-treat
#> contrast for course passing.
#> Under the normal working model with flat priors on the mean and the
#> between-site standard deviation, the informativeness of the 32 sites
#> for course passing was 0.67 (95% posterior interval 0.50 to 0.81), and
#> the posterior probability that it exceeded 0.5 was 0.97.
#> At an informativeness of 0.5, the between-site variance equals the
#> geometric mean of the sampling variances.
#> The mean reliability was 0.66 (0.50 to 0.80).
#> The dispersion of the site reliabilities was H = 0.025 (0.019 to
#> 0.029), with logit variance V = 0.24, and the concentration count was
#> 31.2 (at most 32, the number of sites).
#> These summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors, and
#> each site counts equally in them, whatever its size.

report_table() gives the main numbers as a table, either as a data frame or as markdown or LaTeX text. In an R Markdown document, a chunk with the option results = "asis" turns the markdown into a table:

cat(report_table(fit, format = "markdown"))
J I [95% interval] Mean reliability H [95% interval] J_eff Pr(I > 0.5)
32 .67 [.50, .81] .66 .025 [.019, .029] 31.2 .97

Note. Each estimate is modeled as normal around its site’s effect with a known sampling variance, and the site effects as independent and normal across sites. Flat priors on the mean and the between-site standard deviation. The effects are on the risk difference scale. The estimand at each site is the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course passing. Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors, and each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.

Other vignettes

  • vignette("multisite-trial") adds the study’s second outcome, credits earned by the fourth year, whose diagnostics differ sharply from those of passing, and shows how much the scale of the effects matters.
  • vignette("reliability-profiles") works through the geometry behind II, HH and JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}}.
  • vignette("posterior-summaries") covers the choice of prior, posterior draws from other software and the numerical checks.
  • vignette("meta-analysis") and vignette("small-area-estimation") apply the diagnostics to a meta-analysis and to an area-level model.
  • vignette("planning") uses them to plan a trial.
  • vignette("implementation") documents the computation.
